segments.line: First, you need a kitchen. And it turns out Rome already has fast food.
All over the city, there are little street counters with big clay pots sunk into the stone,
selling hot food to people whose apartments don't even have kitchens.
In Pompeii alone, archaeologists have found about eighty of them. That's real.
One of those counters, right next to the giant race track called the Circus Maximus, belongs to a widow named Tullia.
Business is terrible. Her son Felix is sweeping an empty floor.
You unwrap your cold burger and cut it into three.
Tullia chews.
Felix chews.
Silence. Then Tullia rolls up her sleeves.
Building a burger in Rome is harder than it sounds. Bread is easy. The bakers here make beautiful loaves. You just ask for them round.
Cheese? Rome loves cheese. Lettuce and onions? No problem.
The meat is trickier. Cows here pull ploughs, so you use pork.
Then Tullia shows you an old recipe. Minced meat, pepper, pine nuts and fish sauce, pressed into a patty.
A Roman cookbook really has one. That's real.
Rome basically invented the burger. It just forgot the bun.
Ketchup is impossible. Tomatoes come from the Americas, and nobody will bring them to Europe for another fourteen hundred years.
Same with potatoes, so no fries. You try turnip fries instead.
Felix spits his into a pot.
But your real secret isn't the food. It's the system.
One grill. One job per person. A painted menu with pictures, because a lot of people here can't read.
Clay tokens with numbers, so nobody fights over whose order is next.
You set the price at two bronze coins. In Pompeii, a cup of wine cost one.
The first day, you sell forty burgers. The third day, four hundred.
By the end of the week, the line goes around the block, and a gladiator asks if he can marry Tullia.
